title: Community Medicine I: Health Systems and Primary Health Care in Nigeria
description: Nigeria's health system and financing, primary health care delivery, maternal and child health programmes, immunisation, and health indicators.

topics.title: The Nigerian Health System
topics.summary: WHO health system building blocks, levels of care, and health governance in Nigeria.

notes.b: WHO describes six building blocks of a health system: service delivery; health workforce; health information systems; access to essential medicines, vaccines and technologies; health financing; and leadership and governance. The goals are improved health, responsiveness, financial protection and efficiency. Nigeria's National Health Act (2014) provides the legal framework, including the Basic Health Care Provision Fund (BHCPF — at least 1% of the Consolidated Revenue Fund) to support primary care, emergency care and health insurance for the poor.

Nigeria has three tiers: primary health care — the responsibility of local governments (with state PHC boards under 'PHC Under One Roof' and the NPHCDA nationally) through health posts, PHC centres and comprehensive health centres; secondary care — state governments (general hospitals); and tertiary care — mainly the federal government (teaching hospitals, federal medical centres, specialist hospitals). Referral should flow upwards and counter-referral back down, but many patients bypass PHC, overloading tertiary hospitals. The private sector (including faith-based and informal providers such as patent medicine vendors and traditional healers) delivers a large share of care.
k: PHC: LGAs; secondary: states; tertiary: federal

topics.title: Health Financing and Insurance
topics.summary: Sources of health funds, out-of-pocket spending, the National Health Insurance Authority and UHC.

notes.b: Health financing involves revenue collection (taxes, insurance contributions, out-of-pocket payments, donors), pooling of funds and purchasing of services. In Nigeria, out-of-pocket payments account for roughly 70% of current health expenditure — among the highest in the world — pushing many households into catastrophic spending and poverty. Government health spending is low relative to the Abuja Declaration target (2001) of allocating at least 15% of the annual budget to health. Donor funding supports programmes such as HIV, TB, malaria and immunisation (e.g. the Global Fund, Gavi, PEPFAR).
k: Abuja Declaration: 15% of budget to health

notes.b: The National Health Insurance Scheme (established 1999, launched 2005) was replaced by the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA Act 2022), which makes health insurance mandatory for all Nigerians and supports state social health insurance schemes and a Vulnerable Group Fund for the poor. Health maintenance organisations (HMOs) purchase services. Universal health coverage means all people receive needed quality services without financial hardship — measured by service coverage and financial protection (SDG target 3.8). Community-based health insurance and pooling protect informal sector workers, who make up most of the workforce.
k: Informal sector coverage is a challenge

topics.title: Maternal and Child Health Programmes
topics.summary: Antenatal care, skilled birth attendance, maternal mortality, and child survival strategies.

notes.b: Nigeria has one of the highest maternal mortality ratios in the world (an estimated several hundred to over 1,000 deaths per 100,000 live births in recent estimates) and accounts for a large share of global maternal deaths. Major direct causes: postpartum haemorrhage (leading cause), hypertensive disorders (pre-eclampsia/eclampsia), sepsis, obstructed labour and unsafe abortion. The 'three delays' model: delay in deciding to seek care, delay in reaching care, and delay in receiving adequate care at the facility. WHO recommends at least eight antenatal contacts, with interventions such as iron–folic acid supplementation, tetanus–diphtheria vaccination, IPTp with SP, HIV testing and PMTCT, syphilis screening and birth preparedness. Skilled birth attendance and emergency obstetric care (basic and comprehensive EmONC) reduce deaths.
k: PPH: leading cause of maternal death

notes.b: Leading causes of under-five deaths in Nigeria: neonatal conditions (prematurity, birth asphyxia, neonatal sepsis), pneumonia, diarrhoea, malaria and measles, with malnutrition underlying many deaths. Child survival strategies: GOBI-FFF (Growth monitoring, Oral rehydration, Breastfeeding, Immunisation; Family planning, Female education, Food supplementation), Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) and its community version (iCCM), essential newborn care (clean cord care — chlorhexidine gel, thermal care, early breastfeeding), kangaroo mother care for low-birth-weight babies, vitamin A supplementation, deworming, ORS and zinc for diarrhoea, amoxicillin for pneumonia, and insecticide-treated nets.
k: Chlorhexidine cord care; kangaroo mother care

topics.title: Immunisation Programmes and Disease Eradication
topics.summary: EPI history, the NPI schedule, polio eradication in Nigeria, and vaccine coverage challenges.

notes.b: The Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) was launched by WHO in 1974 and in Nigeria in 1979; it was relaunched as the National Programme on Immunization (NPI) in 1997 and is now managed by the NPHCDA. Routine vaccines protect against tuberculosis (BCG), polio (OPV and IPV), diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b (pentavalent), pneumococcal disease (PCV), rotavirus, measles (MCV1 at 9 months and MCV2 at 15 months), yellow fever, meningococcal A (MenA) and HPV (girls 9–14 years, from 2023). Coverage is measured by indicators such as the proportion of children receiving DPT3/Penta3 and MCV1; 'zero-dose' children (no pentavalent dose) are concentrated in the north and in hard-to-reach communities.
k: Penta3 and MCV1 as coverage indicators

notes.b: The Global Polio Eradication Initiative (1988) uses high routine coverage, supplementary immunisation activities (national immunisation days), acute flaccid paralysis surveillance (in children under 15 — two stool samples 24 hours apart within 14 days of onset) and environmental surveillance of sewage. Nigeria faced setbacks, including the 2003–2004 boycott of polio vaccination in some northern states, but engaged traditional and religious leaders; the WHO certified the African Region free of wild poliovirus in August 2020. Circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2) outbreaks continue in areas of low immunity and are responded to with the novel OPV2 (nOPV2). Smallpox was declared eradicated globally in 1980.
k: AFP surveillance: 2 stools 24 h apart within 14 days

topics.title: Health Indicators, Demography and Health Information
topics.summary: Population measures, demographic transition, vital registration, and health information systems.

notes.b: Demography studies population size, composition and distribution. Nigeria is Africa's most populous country, with a young population (a broad-based population pyramid — about 40% under 15 years), high fertility (total fertility rate around 5 children per woman in recent NDHS surveys) and rapid urbanisation. The demographic transition model describes movement from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates; Nigeria is in an early–middle stage. The dependency ratio = (population aged < 15 + > 64) ÷ population aged 15–64 × 100. Sources of population data: census (last conducted in 2006), vital registration (births and deaths — incomplete in Nigeria, managed by the National Population Commission), surveys (Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey — NDHS, MICS) and health facility data.

The National Health Management Information System (NHMIS) collects routine facility data using DHIS2 platforms; data quality depends on completeness, timeliness, accuracy and consistency. Key indicators: life expectancy, infant mortality rate, under-five mortality rate, maternal mortality ratio, stunting prevalence, immunisation coverage, contraceptive prevalence rate, and skilled birth attendance. Disability-adjusted life years (DALYs = years of life lost + years lived with disability) measure disease burden, combining mortality and morbidity. Data should be used for planning, monitoring and evaluation.
